essays.stem: A friend plans to open a physiotherapy clinic in Mandeville and asks what her business plan must contain to win a bank loan. Explain the sections you would advise and why each matters to the lender.
essays.modelAnswer: I would advise an executive summary first, giving the service, the market, the team, the funding needed and how it will be repaid, because the loan officer reads it to decide whether to read on. A business description would state the clinic's vision, mission, legal structure and objectives, showing what success means. The market analysis would use research on the number of likely patients, referral sources such as doctors and insurers, and competing clinics, which shows that demand is real. The marketing section would set out prices, how patients will be attracted and the clinic's advantage. The operations section would cover the premises, equipment, opening hours, suppliers and the licences and professional registration needed. The management section would show her qualifications and those of any staff, because lenders lend to people they trust to deliver. The financial plan is the part the bank studies most: start-up costs, sources of funds, a sales forecast, a projected income statement, a monthly cash flow forecast for at least a year, break-even and the key assumptions. A risk section would show what could go wrong and her responses. Appendices would hold quotations, CVs and letters of support.
markingPoints: Includes an executive summary and business description with objectives
Includes market analysis and marketing sections based on evidence
Includes operations and management sections, including licences and qualifications
Includes a full financial plan with cash flow and assumptions
Explains why each section matters to the lender and includes risks and appendices

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare the market analysis and marketing sections of a business plan for a new parcel courier service between Kingston and Montego Bay.
essays.modelAnswer: For the market analysis, I would define the target customers: small businesses that send goods between the two cities, online sellers, and families sending parcels. I would estimate the size of the market from published business statistics and from a survey of a sample of small firms on how many parcels they send, how often and what they pay now. I would research the competitors, including bus companies that carry parcels, existing couriers and the postal service, looking at their prices, speed, reliability and what customers complain about. I would note trends, such as the growth of online selling, and any rules on carrying goods. From this I would identify the gap the service will fill, for example guaranteed same-day delivery with tracking. In the marketing section I would set out the service offer, the price list with GCT shown at the current rate where it applies, and how customers will book, through an app, phone or drop-off points. I would plan promotion: visits to businesses, social media and partnerships with online sellers. I would set measurable marketing targets, such as 300 business accounts in the first year, with a budget and a timetable.
markingPoints: Defines target customers and estimates market size from evidence
Analyses competitors and identifies the gap or advantage
Notes relevant trends and rules
Sets out the offer, pricing, channels and promotion
Sets measurable marketing targets with a budget and timing

essays.stem: A business plan for a café gives these figures. Start-up costs: equipment J$3,500,000, fit-out J$1,500,000, opening stock J$400,000 and a cash reserve of J$600,000. The owner will put in J$2,000,000 and borrow the rest. Year-one sales are forecast at J$15,000,000, cost of sales at 35% of sales, and overheads, including loan interest, at J$8,250,000. Calculate the loan needed, the gross profit, the net profit and the net profit margin, and comment on whether the plan looks viable if J$800,000 of the loan must be repaid in year one.
essays.modelAnswer: Total start-up costs are J$3,500,000 plus J$1,500,000 plus J$400,000 plus J$600,000, which is J$6,000,000. With J$2,000,000 from the owner, the loan needed is J$4,000,000. Cost of sales is 35% of J$15,000,000, which is J$5,250,000, so gross profit is J$9,750,000. Taking away overheads of J$8,250,000 leaves a net profit of J$1,500,000, a net profit margin of 10%. If J$800,000 of the loan must be repaid in year one, J$700,000 of profit remains, before any tax and any drawings by the owner. The plan therefore looks viable, but with a thin margin of safety. A fall in sales of only about 5% would cut gross profit by roughly J$490,000 and leave little to spare. I would advise the owner to show a monthly cash flow forecast to check that repayments can be met in quiet months, to test the forecast at lower sales, to explain the evidence for J$15,000,000 of sales, and to consider asking the bank for a longer repayment period so that the business has more room in its first year.
markingPoints: Start-up costs J$6,000,000 and loan J$4,000,000 worked correctly
Gross profit J$9,750,000 worked correctly
Net profit J$1,500,000 and margin 10% worked correctly
Recognises J$700,000 left after repayment and a thin margin of safety
Gives sensible advice, such as cash flow checks, sensitivity tests or longer repayment

essays.stem: Evaluate the main legal structures a new business can choose (sole trader, partnership and limited company), and recommend one for three friends starting a software firm in Kingston.
essays.modelAnswer: A sole trader is the simplest structure: one owner, few formalities, and full control and profit. Its weakness is unlimited liability, so the owner's house and savings are at risk if the business fails, and it is hard to raise large sums. A partnership allows two or more people to share skills, money and work, and is still fairly simple to set up. However, partners usually have unlimited liability, each can be bound by the others' business decisions, and disputes can end the business unless there is a clear written partnership agreement. A limited company is registered under company law and is a separate legal person, so the owners' liability is generally limited to what they invest. It can issue shares to bring in investors and often looks more credible to large clients and lenders. Its drawbacks are more formalities: registration, annual returns, proper accounts and more costs. For three friends starting a software firm, I would recommend a limited company. They will sign contracts with clients that carry risk, may need outside investors as they grow, and need clear shareholdings. They should also sign a shareholders' agreement setting out roles, decisions and what happens if one leaves.
markingPoints: Evaluates the sole trader structure with strengths and weaknesses
Evaluates the partnership with strengths and weaknesses, including the need for an agreement
Evaluates the limited company, including limited liability and formalities
Makes a clear recommendation for the software firm
Justifies the recommendation from the firm's situation

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare the operations and management sections of a business plan for a small furniture factory in May Pen.
essays.modelAnswer: For the operations section, I would describe the premises: size, location, access for delivery trucks, power supply and why the site was chosen. I would list the main machines and tools, their cost and capacity, and show how the furniture will be made, step by step, from cutting timber to finishing and delivery. I would name the main suppliers of timber, hardware and finishes, with lead times and back-up suppliers. I would set out the production capacity, for example forty pieces a week, the quality checks at each stage, and how stock and orders will be controlled. I would include the licences, permits and safety and environmental requirements, such as dust control and safe storage of finishes. For the management section, I would show the legal structure and the owners, then an organisation chart with each key role, such as production supervisor, sales officer and bookkeeper. I would give the experience and skills of each key person and show any gaps and how they will be filled, through hiring, training or advisers such as an accountant. Finally, I would give the staffing plan for the first year with numbers, timing and full staff costs, linked to the financial plan.
markingPoints: Describes premises, equipment and the production process
Covers suppliers, capacity, quality and stock control
Includes licences, safety and environmental requirements
Sets out structure, key roles, skills and how gaps will be filled
Gives a staffing plan with costs linked to the financial plan

essays.stem: Explain how a business plan should identify risks and set contingency plans, using examples from a farm tour business in St Elizabeth.
essays.modelAnswer: The plan should first identify the risks that could stop the business reaching its objectives, using the SWOT and PESTLE findings and talks with experienced people. For a farm tour business, these might include a fall in visitor numbers after a hurricane or a downturn overseas, drought damaging the crops that visitors come to see, a visitor injured on the farm, the loss of a key tour operator who supplies most bookings, and rising fuel costs for the tour bus. Each risk should be rated by how likely it is and how much harm it would do, so that the plan focuses on the most serious ones. For each serious risk, the plan should state what will be done to reduce it and what will happen if it occurs. For example, the business could sell to several tour operators and directly online, insure against injury and property damage, follow a safety plan with trained guides and clear paths, keep a water tank and irrigation, and hold a cash reserve for three quiet months. The plan should name who watches each risk, show the cost of the main measures in the financial plan, and say when the risks will be reviewed.
markingPoints: Explains identifying risks from analysis and advice
Gives relevant risks for the farm tour business
Rates risks by likelihood and impact
Sets out preventive measures and contingency actions with examples
Assigns owners, costs the measures and plans regular review

essays.stem: Describe the process of developing a business plan, from gathering information to final approval, and say whom you would consult along the way.
essays.modelAnswer: The process starts with being clear on the purpose of the plan and its readers, for example raising a loan or guiding a new branch. Next comes gathering information: market research on customers and competitors, quotations for equipment and premises, legal and licence requirements, and cost and price information. I would then set the vision, mission and objectives and decide the strategy, using a SWOT analysis of the findings. With the strategy agreed, I would draft each section: marketing, operations, management, risks and the action plan with milestones. The financial plan would follow, built from the other sections so that the figures match what is promised, with clear assumptions and tests at lower sales. Throughout, I would consult the owners or board on goals and limits, key staff on operations and costs, an accountant on the forecasts and tax, an attorney on the legal structure and contracts, and possibly a business support agency or mentor. I would then review the whole draft for consistency, accuracy and clarity, ask someone outside the project to read it, correct it, and present it to the owners or board for approval. Once approved, it would be shared with those who must deliver it.
markingPoints: Clarifies the purpose and readers first
Gathers the market, cost and legal information needed
Sets objectives and strategy, then drafts the sections with the financial plan built from them
Consults suitable people: owners, staff, accountant, attorney, advisers
Reviews the draft, gets approval and shares the plan

essays.stem: Justify why a business plan should be a working document, and explain how an owner should monitor and update it once the business is trading.
essays.modelAnswer: A business plan is written before the business has real results, so many of its figures are informed guesses. Once trading starts, actual sales, costs and customer responses will differ from the forecasts, and the market will change. If the plan is filed away, the owner has no clear way to see whether the business is on track or to spot problems early. Used as a working document, it provides targets to measure against and a guide for decisions. To monitor it, the owner should turn the plan's objectives into monthly targets and key measures, such as sales, gross margin, cash balance and number of customers. Each month she should compare actual results with the plan, look into large differences and agree actions, for example cutting a cost or changing a promotion. Progress against the milestones in the action plan should be checked at the same time. Every quarter she should update the cash flow forecast, and once a year review the whole plan: the market, objectives, strategy and forecasts, and roll it forward another year. She should share updates with the bank or investors where agreed, as this builds trust.
markingPoints: Justifies using the plan as a working document: forecasts differ from reality and markets change
Turns objectives into monthly targets and measures
Compares actual results with the plan and acts on differences
Updates forecasts regularly and reviews the whole plan yearly
Shares updates with lenders or investors where appropriate

essays.stem: Explain how a business plan should be adapted for three different readers: a bank, an equity investor and the firm's own managers.
essays.modelAnswer: The core of the plan, its facts and figures, must be the same for every reader, because honesty matters and readers may compare versions. What changes is the emphasis and the level of detail. A bank lends money that must be repaid with interest, so its main concern is safety. For a bank I would stress the cash flow forecast, the ability to meet repayments in quiet months, the security offered, the owners' own investment and the experience of the team. An equity investor shares in the risk and the reward, so they want to see growth. For an investor I would stress the size and growth of the market, the competitive advantage, the plans to expand, the expected return and how they could eventually sell their share, as well as what share and say they will have. The firm's own managers need the plan to guide their work. For them I would stress the objectives, the strategies, the action plan with milestones and responsibilities, and the targets and budgets for their areas, with less focus on funding terms. In every version I would keep the summary short and the figures consistent.
markingPoints: States that the facts and figures stay the same; only emphasis and detail change
Explains the bank's focus on repayment, cash flow and security
Explains the investor's focus on growth, return and exit
Explains the managers' focus on objectives, actions and responsibilities
Gives a clear, practical approach for preparing each version

essays.stem: Explain how the objectives and strategies in a business plan should link to the vision and to the findings of a SWOT analysis, using an example from a small hotel in Treasure Beach.
essays.modelAnswer: The vision states where the business wants to be in the long term, for example "to be the best-known small eco-hotel on the south coast". The objectives turn this into measurable targets for the plan period, such as "reach 70% average occupancy and a guest rating of at least 9 out of 10 by the end of year two". The strategies are the main ways the objectives will be achieved, and they should be built on the SWOT findings. Suppose the SWOT shows strengths of a quiet beach location and friendly local staff, a weakness of low online visibility, an opportunity in the growing demand for nature and community tourism, and a threat from new villas listed on rental websites. Sensible strategies would use the strengths to take the opportunity, for example creating packages with local fishermen and farm tours, and tackle the weakness, for example by improving the website and online reviews. The threat could be met by offering experiences that villas cannot. Each strategy then leads to actions with owners and dates in the action plan, and to costs in the financial plan, so that the whole plan is consistent from vision to figures.
markingPoints: Explains the vision and gives a relevant example
Shows objectives as measurable targets derived from the vision
Shows strategies built on SWOT findings, using strengths and opportunities and tackling weaknesses and threats
Uses a realistic example for the hotel
Links strategies to actions and the financial plan for consistency

practical1.title: Write the main sections of a business plan for a new venture
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a short case for a made-up new business (for example a mobile physiotherapy service in Spanish Town, a cassava bammy bakery in St Elizabeth, or a computer repair shop in Mandeville), with some market research results, quotations and the owners' goals. As a group, write the non-financial sections of its business plan, about six to eight pages: an executive summary (written last), a business description with vision, mission, legal structure and three SMART objectives, a market analysis, a marketing section, an operations section, a management and staffing section with an organisation chart, a risk section with at least five risks and responses, and an action plan with milestones. Give each member a named role: plan editor (keeps the group to time, writes the executive summary and checks the sections agree), market writer (market analysis and marketing), operations writer (operations section), people writer (management, staffing and organisation chart), and risk and action planner (risk section and action plan). In a group of four, the plan editor also writes the business description. Photograph each stage and hand in the plan once for the whole group.
materials: Business case, research results and quotations from the assessor
Computers with word-processing software and a printer
photos: The flipchart outline of the plan with each member's sections and deadlines
The vision, mission and SMART objectives on the flipchart
The market analysis and marketing sections on screen
The organisation chart and staffing plan
The risk table and the action plan with milestones
The finished plan with its executive summary
checklist: Took a named role and completed their sections
Objectives are SMART and link to the vision
Market and marketing sections use the evidence given, not guesses
Operations and staffing sections are realistic for the case
Risks are specific, with practical responses
Sections agree with each other and the executive summary reflects the whole plan
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up case and keep the work confidential to the group and the assessor
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Share the writing fairly and agree realistic deadlines for each section
Take short screen breaks and keep cables out of walkways

practical2.title: Prepare the financial plan and defend it before a loan panel
practical2.brief: Using the assessor's case and figures (or the business from Practical 1), your group prepares the financial section of a business plan in a spreadsheet and then defends it before a loan panel. The financial section must include: a table of start-up costs and sources of funds; a twelve-month sales forecast; a projected income statement for year one; a twelve-month cash flow forecast; a break-even calculation; a list of key assumptions; and a test showing the effect of sales 10% below forecast. Every sum must be checked twice by a second member. Then present the financial plan in ten minutes, with no more than five slides, to a panel of two (the assessor and another person playing a loan officer), and answer their questions. Give each member a named role: finance lead (sets up the spreadsheet and checks that the sheets link), sales forecaster (sales forecast and assumptions), cost and profit officer (start-up costs and income statement), cash flow officer (cash flow forecast and break-even), and presenter (leads the presentation, with every member answering at least one question). In a group of four, the finance lead also prepares the sales test. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in the spreadsheet, slides and notes of the panel's questions and answers.
materials: Case figures from the assessor (prices, volumes, costs, loan terms)
Computers with spreadsheet and presentation software, a printer and a projector or large screen
photos: The start-up costs and sources of funds table on screen
The sales forecast and the list of assumptions
The projected income statement and break-even working
The twelve-month cash flow forecast, with the second check marked
The test of sales 10% below forecast
The panel presentation in progress, and the notes of questions and answers
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the financial plan
